1:
The voices agree that this chapter is an appendix and that Jeremiah did not write it. Keil and Delitzsch argue the case: the closing formula of the preceding chapter marks off what follows, and since this account reaches to the liberation of Jehoiachin the prophet can scarcely have lived to compose it; the contents also agree almost word for word with the parallel record in Kings. Wesley reasons the same way, that Jeremiah would not have so largely repeated what he had already related, nor could relate what happened after his time, and guesses at some of the exiles in Babylon, who set it here as a preface to the Lamentations. Clarke names Ezra as the likely hand, and says the chapter is subjoined to the prophecies to show how exactly they were fulfilled. Henry supposes it drawn up by some carried away with Zedekiah, as a reproach to themselves for having hoped they would not go into captivity after their brethren.

On the king Gill supplies what the narrative omits, that his name was Mattaniah and that the king of Babylon set him on the throne in the room of his brother's son. Both Gill and Henry notice that no idolatry is recorded of him; his evil lay in disobeying the word of the Lord and refusing to humble himself before the prophet, and Henry adds that he did evil in not doing the good he should have done. The rebellion against Babylon was the deed that hastened the end, and Henry calls it both sin and folly, ruinous to the people not only in desert but in effect, since God, being angry with Judah, gave the king over to the hand of his own counsels. Clarke states it as an epigram, a king given to a people in God's anger and taken away in his displeasure. Henry reads the casting out from God's presence as expulsion from a land that bore tokens of his bounty and from a temple that bore tokens of his covenant love; yet none are cast out, he says, but those who by sin first threw themselves out.

The siege runs eighteen months, which Gill counts from the tenth day of the tenth month in the ninth year to the ninth day of the fourth in the eleventh; Clarke sets the tenth month at nearly our January and the fourth at nearly our July, and Gill names the latter Tammuz and ties it to the fast later kept for the taking of the city. Henry sets beside it the other fasts of the captivity, the fifth month for the burning of the temple and the seventh for the murder of Gedaliah, and draws from the famine the lesson that walls will not hold out without men, nor men without walls, nor both together without God. Ellicott works through the differences from the parallel narrative, where the date of the fourth month is wanting in the Hebrew, the flight from the city is unmentioned, and judgment is given by an unnamed they rather than by the king of Babylon; the slaying of the princes of Judah is absent there but stands in an earlier chapter of this book. On the prison he observes that the word is peculiar, literally a house of visitation, implying stricter custody or punishment added to it, and that the Greek renders it a house of the mill, as though the blinded king were set to slave work like Samson. Such usage, he adds, suited Assyrian and Chaldean rulers, one of whom boasted of chaining a king of Arabia with the dogs at a gate of Nineveh. Henry sees the same humiliation in the arraignment, a king of the house of David standing as a criminal at the bar of a heathen king, and calls the flight vain from the first, since there is no escaping the judgments of God.
12:
Gill dates the month and attaches the memory to it: the fifth month was Ab, answering to part of July and part of August, and from the burning of the city came the fast kept in that month; Clarke says only that it answers nearly to our August. Ellicott notes that the parallel record gives the seventh day where this gives the tenth, that there is no means of deciding between them, and that the commemorative fast has always been kept on the ninth, a date supported by one of the old versions. He also corrects the description of the captain of the guard, whose title is better rendered as one who stands before the king, a phrase used continually of honourable service, where the parallel uses a less accurate word.

Henry follows the destruction item by item, and pauses on the marginal title given to Nebuzaradan, the chief of the slaughter-men or executioners, since soldiers are but slaughter-men whom God employs as executioners of his sentence against a sinful people; he adds that this one, for all that, had no eye to God but served the king of Babylon and his own designs. He burnt the house of the Lord, having first plundered it of everything valuable; he burnt the royal palace, probably the house that Solomon built after the temple; he burnt the houses of the great men, and if any escaped it was only some sorry cottages of the poor; and he broke down the walls, Henry thinks in revenge for the delay the city had cost his army, so that of a defenced city it was made a ruin. Ellicott sharpens one phrase here, reading not all the houses of the great men but all the great houses. How long the temple had stood is disputed among the voices: Gill reports a computation of four hundred and seventy years, six months and ten days on the authority of Josephus, with a rabbinic reckoning of four hundred and ten beside it, while Clarke states four hundred and twenty-four years, three months and eight days and gives dates for the building and the burning.

The two classes of poor cause a textual difficulty. Gill harmonises them, taking the poor carried off as the poor of the city and those left behind as the poor of the country, who had not been concerned in defending it. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott agree instead that the opening words of the verse are wanting in the parallel and have been brought in by an error of the copyist from the beginning of the next verse, since the poor of the land are the subject there and are left in the country, while this verse treats of those carried to Babylon. Ellicott offers a further possibility for the last clause, that instead of the rest of the multitude we should read the remnant of the work-people, though he concedes the old versions agree in multitude. Clarke identifies those that fell away as the deserters to the Chaldeans during the siege.

Keil and Delitzsch explain why the great brazen furniture was broken rather than carried: the pillars of the porch, the bases and the sea were too vast in their proportions to be moved to Babylon, so the Chaldeans broke them up and took the metal, and he judges this account of the vessels fuller and more precise than the parallel. Gill names the two pillars Jachin and Boaz, made of cast brass, and identifies the caldrons as the pots of bright brass in which the flesh of the sacrifices was boiled; of the basons he notes that they were of gold and that the parallel omits them.
20:
Gill carries the inventory alone. The two pillars are Jachin and Boaz, named before, and the sea is the molten sea with the twelve oxen it stood upon. On the measurements he registers a difficulty rather than hiding it, since the height of one pillar is given here as eighteen cubits and elsewhere as thirty-five, and he refers the reader to the reconciliation offered in another place. The chapiter he describes as a coronet of molten brass set on the top of the pillar, and the ninety-six pomegranates he explains from the Hebrew, which reads to the wind, that is toward the four winds, twenty-four to each corner, which make up the number.

With the officers the narrative turns from furniture to men. Gill supposes Seraiah taken out of the temple, where he was either ministering or had fled for safety, and reports the tradition that he was the father of Ezra. Clarke identifies the three keepers of the door as the priests who stood there to receive the offerings of the people, and Wesley adds that there were probably more of them, the captain of the guard taking only three of the chief. Gill makes the eunuch the muster-master-general of the army, and Clarke makes the seven near the king privy counsellors. Ellicott works from the Hebrew: the word rendered charge means a deputy, a superintendent serving under a chief commander, and the description of the men as those near the king's person is literally that they saw the king's face, which implies high official rank. He also marks that the parallel record numbers these five where this numbers seven, and finds a principle running through the whole list, that prominence in the defence of the city was what the exile punished; the chief scribe of the army, the secretary of war, would naturally have stood in that position.

Henry counts the slaughter at Riblah and finds it seventy-two in cold blood, the number of the elders of Israel, made up in the parallel of five out of the temple, two out of the city, five out of the court and sixty out of the country. He notices the same discrepancy that Ellicott does, seven here against five there, and reports a proposed reconciliation, that seven were taken from about the king but two of them were afterwards discharged, so that only five were put to death and the total holds. He supposes that those made examples of had been the most forward in exciting the rebellion against the king of Babylon, and that Seraiah stands first because his sacred character could not exempt him from the stroke, since he had himself profaned it by sin; the leaders had caused the people to err, and are now in a particular manner made monuments of divine justice. Gill notes that the king ordered them smitten with the sword and that a historian says their heads were cut off. Henry closes the section on the summary sentence that Judah was carried away captive out of his own land, and hears in it the older warning that the land would spue them out as it had spued out the Canaanites before them if they trod in their steps and copied their abominations.
28:
Ellicott marks the seam. Here the parallelism with the older history ceases, since that book goes on to summarise the story of Gedaliah, and the writer of this appendix turns instead to particulars about the stages of the deportation. The particulars raise difficulties at once, and every voice registers them. Gill notes that the seventh year is given elsewhere as the eighth, and reports a Jewish commentator's reconciliation, that the event fell at the end of the one and the beginning of the other; he repeats the same solution for the eighteenth year, which is elsewhere the nineteenth, and offers a second possibility for that one, that this was the deportation made before the city fell, when the besieging king raised the siege and marched to meet the king of Egypt.

Clarke sets out at length the reasoning of another writer, whose substance he extracts. The totals cannot be the whole of the captivity, since more than twice four thousand six hundred were carried away at one time, and before that a number had gone from Jerusalem in the first year of the reign, among them Daniel and his companions, who are not noticed here at all; nor can the eight hundred and thirty-two answer to the taking and burning of the city, which this chapter itself dates to the nineteenth year. There are therefore three great deportations, in the first, eighth and nineteenth years, and these three in the seventh, eighteenth and twenty-third are quite distinct from them, and are best understood as removals of a minor kind not elsewhere recorded in direct terms. The first would be of prisoners picked up in various parts of Judah by the bands of Chaldeans and Syrians sent against the land before the king came in person; the second belongs to the moment when the Chaldean army broke off the siege to meet the Egyptian army, and might naturally send off the prisoners then in camp under guard; the third falls when the king, being engaged in the siege of Tyre, sent his captain against the Moabites and Ammonites, who swept up the gleanings of the Jews left in their own land.

Ellicott proposes a different repair. The precision of the number three thousand and twenty-three implies a register of some kind and so looks accurate on its face, whereas the older book gives ten thousand for the first deportation; probably the word ten has dropped out before seven, so that what we have is the record of a second removal in the seventeenth year, while the siege was still going on, made up partly of prisoners taken in skirmishes and partly of the many who fell away to the Chaldeans. Of the eight hundred and thirty-two he observes that so small a figure measures the ravages of sword and pestilence and famine, and takes the captives for the scanty remnant of the defenders. For the last deportation, five years after the city fell, he notes there is no record in the historical books at all, and suggests it followed the conquest of Egypt and swept in some who had emigrated there, and perhaps some sheltering among the Moabites and Edomites. Gill has the same year given by Jewish tradition as the year Tyre fell, and reports another account, that these were the poor of the land taken in revenge for the murder of Gedaliah. Ellicott then presses the totals further: even at fourteen thousand six hundred they will not account for the more than forty thousand recorded as returning afterwards, which suggests that once the exiles were settled and found their position better than they had feared, friends and kindred came out and joined them. Wesley draws the plainer moral from the same arithmetic, that the people were amazingly diminished if this handful was all that went into captivity.
31:
Gill does the arithmetic: the king was eighteen when carried away, so he is fifty-five now. Ellicott finds the closing narrative almost identical with its parallel, differing only in a day of the month, a fuller title for the king of Babylon, and a pleonastic clause before the last words; and he draws a general conclusion from such variations, that though insignificant in themselves they show that belief in the substantial truthfulness of the historical records does not depend on verbal accordance in minute detail. Henry meets the two-day difference by supposing the orders for release given on one day and the prisoner presented to the king on the other. Clarke explains the idiom of the release: to lift up the head rests on the observation that men in sorrow hold their heads down and raise them when the cause of grief is removed, and in Hebrew the phrase signifies to comfort, to cheer, to make happy.

Henry finds four things in the story. First, that new lords make new laws. The old king had kept this unhappy prince in prison, and his son, though well affected to him, could win him no favour while his father lived, any more than Jonathan could for David; when the peevish old man was dead the son made him a favourite. It is common, Henry adds, for children to undo what their fathers did, and it were well if it were always as much for the better as this. Second, that this is a changing world: he fell from a throne into a prison and is advanced again to a throne of state, though not of power, his robes turned into prison garments and back into robes, such chequer-work being this world, where prosperity and adversity are set one over against the other so that we may learn to rejoice as though we rejoiced not. Third, that though the night of affliction be long we must not despair of the dawn; thirty-seven years a prisoner from the age of eighteen, he may be supposed either inured to captivity or all the more glad of liberty, and those whose afflictions have been lengthened out may take the encouragement. Fourth, that God can make his people find favour with their oppressors and unaccountably turn their hearts to pity them.

Gill and Clarke fill in the kindness. To speak kindly is literally to speak good things to him, and Gill notes that the king comforted him and promised him favours, and was as good as his word; Clarke says he conversed freely with him and gave him a better seat than the other captive princes, probably near his own person. The prison garments Gill describes as filthy and of an ill smell, exchanged for raiment suitable to his dignity and fit to appear in at court; Clarke reads the clause as the king changing his own garments to match his elevation, and recalls that robes were commonly given in token of favour. Of the allowance Gill says it covered not food only but provision for his household and servants, and Clarke calls it a ration for that household. Clarke also doubts the final clause, which he thinks tautologous here and probably carried over by mistake from the verse before, since it is wanting in the Greek and the Arabic, and he prefers an older English rendering that ends the book, all the days of his life until he died. Wesley closes by noting that the history of the kingdom ends here, and sets the census numbers of Judah and Benjamin and half Manasseh, once well over a hundred thousand, against the four thousand and six hundred carried into captivity, so that one may judge what a multitude had been consumed by sword and famine and pestilence; it is a dreadful thing, he says, to mock God's messengers and misuse his prophets till there be no remedy.
